transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. As we prepare for the first case-management conference three weeks from now, I need to review our draft litigation plan before I approve it. I understand the current draft preserves both asserted claims — claim 7 and claim 12 — seeks broad technical discovery, and permits source-code production under the opposing party's proposed protective order. Before I sign off, I need both of you to report any facts that should change this draft plan. Are there any issues with either of the asserted claims, the discovery scope, or the protective order terms that I should know about?

transcript.text: Elena, there is a fact that should change the draft plan. Yesterday, while reviewing a newly indexed prior-art collection, I found a published 2016 software implementation that anticipates every limitation of claim 7. Under our litigation policy, this requires claim 7 to be withdrawn from the asserted-claims strategy. My separate review found no equivalent anticipation of claim 12, so claim 12 should remain. I had not revised the draft plan because the prior-art collection was indexed after the plan circulated. The plan should be updated to withdraw claim 7, and discovery should be limited to material relevant to the surviving claim 12.

transcript.text: Elena, there's an issue with the protective order that should change the draft plan. I confirmed with the engineering security team this week that the proposed protective order is inadequate for our source code — it allows two named employees of the opposing party to access produced code. Our board-approved security policy requires that source-code access be limited to outside counsel and independent experts who have signed enhanced source-code acknowledgments. I hadn't yet updated the litigation plan because the security team's confirmation arrived after our last legal-team meeting. The plan should be revised to require a protective order that complies with our security policy before any source-code production occurs.
